text: @arv/structs is an implementation of the TC39 structs proposal (Stage 2, the December 2024 draft) for JavaScript today: structs, shared structs, Shared Arrays, Atomics.Mutex and Atomics.Condition. It has a runtime that follows the spec's algorithms, and a compiler for the proposal's syntax. In TypeScript, the compiler also uses the types to make shared struct field access direct. shared struct Counter { count = 0; lock = new Atomics.Mutex(); } const counter = new Counter(); worker.postMessage(counter); // the same object in the worker, not a copy // in any agent: { using _ = Atomics.Mutex.lock(counter.lock); counter.count++; } You can write programs and run them in your browser, with the compiled JavaScript side by side, in the playground. Status: experimental This is the tc39-proposal branch of arv/threads. It replaces the threads library on main with something much smaller that stays as close to the spec as JavaScript allows. See Differences from the Spec.

Spec Here §1 struct declarations The compiler lowers them to classes that call the runtime §2 shared struct declarations Proxies over one growable SharedArrayBuffer, the heap §2.3 Atomics on struct fields load, store, exchange and compareExchange take a struct §2.4 Reflect.canBeShared Installed on Reflect §3 SharedArray A global: a Shared Struct with indexed fields and a fixed length §4 Atomics.Mutex, UnlockToken Futex-style locks on heap words; tokens work with using §4 Atomics.Condition wait, waitFor (with a timeout and a predicate), notify Importing @arv/structs installs the globals. The compiler's output imports @arv/structs/runtime, which does it too.
Running It: the Node hook, the CLI and the compiler's API. Structs and Shared Structs: what the syntax makes, and how. The Playground: try it all in your browser.

Where JavaScript can't do what the spec says, or where the spec text looks like an oversight, this implementation does something else: Memory is never reclaimed. Shared objects and interned strings live until the process ends. There is no collector across agents. Symbols. Only registered (Symbol.for) and well-known symbols can be shared, as values or as field keys, because other agents don't have the others. Reflect.canBeShared returns false for the rest. [[GetOwnProperty]] reports shared fields as writable. The spec says not writable, but its own [[DefineOwnProperty]] asserts writable, and a Proxy can't report a writable target property as non-writable. Constructors are classes. A shared struct's constructor has a prototype object (with a null prototype; its instances still have none). A struct with no extends has a hidden root function as its constructor's [[Prototype]], not Function.prototype. Arguments. The spec evaluates the arguments of new S(...) and of super(...) but never passes them to the initializer. Here they are passed. Static methods are not brand-checked. The spec's DefineMethod would wrap them too, which would make them impossible to call. Computed instance field keys are evaluated when the static elements start, not in element order. super.x in a shared struct's initializers looks at the parent constructor. In the spec their home object is null, and super.x throws. Mutexes aren't fair. A woken waiter competes with newcomers, where the spec has a waiter queue. Logging a shared struct in Node Node's console.log shows a Proxy's target, so it prints a shared struct's fields as undefined. Spread it instead: console.log({...s}).

Atomics.Mutex and Atomics.Condition are shared structs with no fields, so they can be stored in another shared struct's fields and sent to workers. A lock gives an UnlockToken, which using unlocks at the end of its block. A Condition waits with that token: it unlocks the Mutex while it waits and locks it again before it returns. shared struct Queue { items = new SharedArray(16); size = 0; lock = new Atomics.Mutex(); changed = new Atomics.Condition(); } // on a worker: wait until there is something to take { using token = Atomics.Mutex.lock(queue.lock); Atomics.Condition.waitFor(queue.changed, token, Infinity, () => queue.size > 0); // take an item, then tell the others Atomics.Condition.notify(queue.changed); } Atomics.load, store, exchange and compareExchange also take a shared struct and a field name (§2.3), for lock-free code on its fields. The code is in src/runtime/sync.ts and src/runtime/atomics.ts.

@arv/structs is the tc39-proposal branch of arv/threads. The repository is a pnpm workspace on Vite+ (vp), with the playground and these docs as packages of their own. pnpm install vp check vp test vp check formats, lints and type checks. vp test runs the tests in test/, including workers that share the heap, and the site's own: every link of these docs leads somewhere, and every code block and table of the repository's Markdown is in them.

In Node, the register hook compiles struct syntax as modules load, in workers too: node --import @arv/structs/register examples/counter/main.js The CLI compiles a single file, or a whole TypeScript project with type checking: node src/compiler/cli.ts transpile examples/counter/main.js node src/compiler/cli.ts compile -p examples/nbody/tsconfig.json compile writes each file to the tsconfig's outDir (or build/), with its source map. --no-fast leaves every shared struct field access to the Proxy (see TypeScript), and --typescript keeps the types. From code, use transpile(source, {fileName}) and compile(tsconfigPath) from @arv/structs/compiler. The compiler runs on TypeScript 7 It parses with TypeScript 7's API, the same parser for JavaScript and for TypeScript, which starts tsgo, TypeScript's compiler, as a process. The playground runs the same compiler on tsgo in WebAssembly.

Every agent attaches to one growable SharedArrayBuffer. A Shared Struct is a block in it with a slot per field. Each agent sees the block through a Proxy whose traps are the spec's internal methods (§2.1.5 to §2.1.10). There is one Proxy per block per agent, so === holds. a shared object [kind][shape: its keys, interned][..][..] then 16 bytes per field a slot [a tagged word: the value][a Float64, for a Number] A field holds undefined, null, a boolean, a Number, a string (interned in the heap), a BigInt, a registered or well-known symbol, or another shared object. Anything else is a TypeError (CanBeSharedAcrossAgents, §2.2.4). A read never tears: a Number's Float64 is written before its word, and the word is stored atomically. Mutex and Condition are Shared Structs with no fields. Their internal slots are heap words that Atomics.wait and Atomics.notify work on. Blocking where an agent cannot (a browser's main thread) is a TypeError, as the spec says (AgentCanSuspend). The code is in src/runtime/heap.ts (the heap) and src/runtime/shared.ts (slots, shapes and the Proxies).

The proposal leaves sharing across agents to the host. @arv/structs/agent starts workers that attach to the same heap: worker_threads in Node, module Web Workers in a browser. Messages sent through it carry shared objects as themselves, and everything else as postMessage copies it. // main.js import {startWorker} from '@arv/structs/agent'; const w = startWorker(new URL('./worker.js', import.meta.url)); w.postMessage({tally, n: 1000}); // worker.js import {parent} from '@arv/structs/agent'; parent.onmessage = ({tally, n}) => { /* tally is the main thread's struct */ }; run(url, name, ...args) calls the function a module exports as name on a new worker and settles with what it returns. A module can run its own functions with run(import.meta.url, ...). examples/counter has four workers counting to a million under a Mutex, with a Condition saying when they are done.

A struct is a class with a different construction. The compiler keeps the class, which gives the struct its scope, private names and static elements. It moves the fields and the constructor into the runtime's hands (src/runtime/structs.ts shows the shape). An instance is made the spec's way (§1.1.6): All of its fields, the base struct's first, are defined as undefined, and it is sealed. The field initializers run, from the base struct down. The constructor runs. It is an initializer, and super(...) calls the parent struct's initializer. Instance methods check that this is an instance of their struct (struct method exotic objects, §1.2). Constructing anything but the struct itself is a TypeError, so a class cannot extend a struct. No constructor, no initializer A struct with no constructor has no initializer, so its parent's initializer doesn't run. That's the spec's behavior. Classes do the opposite.
The playground is a page where you write programs in the proposal's syntax, see what they compile to, and run them on Web Workers that share memory. Its source is in playground/.

Pick a program from the Program menu and edit it in Monaco. As you type, the page compiles the program and shows you: The JavaScript. Direct field access shows what the compiler emits where TypeScript proves an object is an instance of a shared struct: the field is read and written in shared memory, without the Proxy. Proxy only shows the same program with every field access going through the Proxy. The runtime's calls are marked, and the direct accesses are in bold. The errors. These are TypeScript's, from seeing each struct as a class, and the structs' own: a shared struct can't have methods, for example. They appear as squiggles in the editor and in a list. The output. Run calls the program's main(workers) on a worker, with the number in the Workers field. main may block, on Atomics.Mutex.lock for example. A program starts its own workers with run(import.meta.url, 'name', ...args) from @arv/structs/agent, which calls the function it exports as name on a new worker. Their console output comes back to the page. Stop ends the run, along with the workers it started. Monaco's TypeScript can't parse struct, so the editor only colors and completes. The errors you see come from the playground's compiler. The page remembers your edits to each program in this browser. Reset puts the original back.

You need Node 22.13 or later and a recent Chrome. A static build also needs Go 1.27 or later, and git. vp install vp dev playground On the dev server, programs compile in Node, on TypeScript's native API. Add ?wasm to the address to compile in the browser instead.

Without a dev server, the page compiles programs itself. It runs the same compiler, in a worker, on tsgo (stock TypeScript 7.1) compiled to WebAssembly, in a worker of its own. The two talk over pipes in shared memory. You get the same JavaScript and the same errors as on the dev server. The catch is size: tsgo is 46 MB, about 10 MB gzipped, and the page shows the download as it goes. vp run build-wasm vp build vp run test-build build-wasm builds tsgo from TypeScript's sources at the commit of the compiler's typescript package, into public/compiler/. vp build builds the page into dist/, to be served from /playground/ (set BASE for another path). test-build serves the build with no COOP or COEP headers, so the service worker has to isolate it. It then compiles and runs every program in Chrome, in both modes, and checks that the JavaScript, the errors and the output match the dev server's. Cross-origin isolation SharedArrayBuffer needs a cross-origin isolated page, which takes the COOP and COEP headers. The dev and preview servers send them. Where a host can't, as on GitHub Pages, a service worker adds them, and the page loads once more under it.

Each program exports main(workers): Structs: sealed, initialized in one shot, with brand-checked methods Shared structs across workers: a linked list that workers add to Atomics.Mutex: workers counting together Atomics.Condition: a bounded queue between producers and a consumer Atomics on fields: claiming work with compareExchange N-body: direct field access against the Proxy The mistakes the compiler catches

compile type checks a project as TypeScript sees it with each struct spelled as a class. It drops the errors that hold for a class but not for a struct, such as a derived constructor without super(). Then, where the checker proves an expression is an instance of a shared struct whose fields are all known, o.x and o.x = v skip the Proxy: const dx = a.x - b.x; // compiles to const dx = $struct.getNumber(a, $L0, 0) - $struct.getNumber(b, $L0, 0); The types are not trusted. The runtime checks that the object is a Shared Struct with that layout, and reads it through the Proxy if not, so a structurally typed plain object still works. On examples/nbody (1,000,000 steps, Node 24, Apple Silicon) this takes 2.5 s against the Proxy's 5.0 s. Plain JavaScript objects take about 0.07 s. Closing that gap means letting compiled code hold heap addresses instead of Proxies, as the compiler on main does. The code is in src/compiler/project.ts (the type check) and src/compiler/fast.ts (the direct access).
